## Report: Do anti-cytokine drugs reduce depressive symptoms in chronic inflammatory disease?

Your skepticism is understandable, but the claim is not straightforwardly false—it's a mixed picture depending on population and how "depression" is measured.

**Evidence supporting the claim:** The most cited evidence is Kappelmann et al.'s 2018 systematic review/meta-analysis in *Molecular Psychiatry* (https://www.nature.com/articles/mp2016167; also https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5794896/), which pooled RCTs of anti-cytokine drugs (mainly anti-TNF agents) in rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, Crohn's disease, and similar conditions, where depression was a *secondary* outcome. It found a small-to-moderate reduction in depressive symptoms compared with placebo, but effects were partly attributable to improvement in the underlying physical illness rather than a direct antidepressant action, and studies had methodological limitations (heterogeneity, short duration, risk of bias).

**Evidence against/complicating the claim:** Trials designed specifically to test anti-cytokine drugs *as antidepressants* in people with treatment-resistant depression (not primarily an inflammatory disease) found no overall benefit. Raison et al.'s RCT of infliximab (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/... via PMC/JAMA Psychiatry summary) showed no difference from placebo overall, with possible benefit only in patients with high baseline inflammation (CRP). A more recent 2024 proof-of-mechanism RCT of a TNF antagonist (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41380-024-02751-x) similarly found effects limited to inflammation-related motivational symptoms in a biomarker-selected subgroup, not general antidepressant efficacy.

**Conclusion:** The claim holds modestly true specifically for patients being treated for inflammatory diseases (arthritis, psoriasis, IBD), where symptom relief is partly secondary to reduced disease burden. It does not generalize to using these drugs as standalone antidepressants in the broader depressed population, and benefits are inconsistent, small, and concentrated in high-inflammation subgroups—so a blanket claim overstates the certainty and generalizability of the effect.
